theme: The burning bush; the divine name I AM; Moses commissioned
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 3:1-4:31. This is the call of Moses. Read it slowly. Pay special attention to what God says about himself, and to each excuse that Moses offers and how God answers it.
settingTheScene: Forty years have passed since Moses fled Egypt. He is now eighty, a shepherd in the desert of Midian, and everything he once hoped to be has been left behind. Then, one day, he sees a bush burning that is not consumed. What follows is one of the most important encounters in the Bible. God reveals his name, announces his plan, and commissions an unwilling servant. Almost everything that comes later in the Old Testament, the exodus, the covenant, the law, the prophets, grows out of this scene.
observation: Moses comes to Horeb, “the mountain of God,” and sees “the angel of the LORD” in a flame of fire in the midst of a bush that is not consumed (3:1-2).
God calls, “Moses, Moses!” and tells him not to come near, “for the place on which you are standing is holy ground” (3:4-5).
God says, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (3:6). Moses hides his face.
“I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry…and I have come down to deliver them” (3:7-8).
Moses asks, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh?” God answers, “But I will be with you” (3:11-12).
Moses asks for God’s name. God says, “I AM WHO I AM…Say this to the people of Israel: I AM has sent me to you” (3:14).
God adds, “The LORD, the God of your fathers…has sent me to you. This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations” (3:15).
Moses offers objections: they will not believe me (4:1), I am not eloquent (4:10). God gives him signs, and reminds him, “Who has made man’s mouth?” (4:11).
God is angry at Moses’ final request, “Oh, my Lord, please send someone else” (4:13), but provides his brother Aaron as a spokesman (4:14-16).
God tells Moses to say to Pharaoh, “Israel is my firstborn son…Let my son go that he may serve me” (4:22-23). The people believe and worship (4:31).
interpretation:
The bush that burns without being consumed is a picture of God himself. Fire is a common symbol of God’s holy presence, and here it burns without destroying what it touches. God’s holiness is dangerous, and yet it does not have to be fatal. That is a hint of what is to come in the tabernacle, and in Christ.

The ground is holy because God is there, not because of anything about the place. Moses is told to take off his sandals. It is a physical way of saying that he is in the presence of someone infinitely greater than he is. Many of the Bible’s accounts of meeting God begin this way, and they end with someone who has been changed.

Now look at how God introduces himself. First as the God of the fathers: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He is the God who made promises. Then as the God who sees, hears, knows, and comes down. These are verbs of nearness, and they are what Israel needs to hear. Then God sends Moses, and the sending is hard, because Moses does not want to go.

Moses’ objections are worth looking at one by one. “Who am I?” is a question of worthiness, and God does not answer it by telling Moses that he is great. He answers by saying, “I will be with you.” The solution to his smallness is God’s presence. “What is your name?” is a question about God’s character, and the answer is the most mysterious in Scripture. “They will not believe me” is a question of credibility, and God gives signs. “I am not eloquent” is a question of ability, and God replies, “Who has made man’s mouth?” Every excuse is met with a reminder of who God is.

The name “I AM WHO I AM” has been studied for thousands of years. It seems to say that God is self-existent: he does not depend on anything else, and he simply is. It also seems to say that he will be what he will be: he is free, and he will show himself faithful. The name connected to it, the LORD (Yahweh), becomes the personal name by which Israel knows him. You will see that name in capital letters throughout your English Bible. Tomorrow’s doctrinal day will look at it more closely.

Finally, notice what God calls Israel: “my firstborn son.” This is the language of family. Before the law, before the covenant at Sinai, God says that Israel is his son. Redemption is not a business arrangement. It is the rescue of a child.
connection: Jesus uses the burning bush to teach about the resurrection (Mark 12:26-27). He also speaks the divine name of himself: “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58), and the “I am” sayings in John (6:35; 8:12; 10:11; 11:25; 14:6). Hebrews 3:1-6 compares Moses and Jesus as faithful servants. Paul says that God’s “power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).
application:
Take off your shoes, so to speak. Before you pray this week, spend a minute simply remembering who you are speaking to.

Identify your own list of excuses: “Who am I? What if they do not listen? I am not good enough.” Read God’s answers to Moses as answers to you.

Say aloud, “I will be with you.” If you can, write it on a card where you will see it.
prayerPrompts: Praise God for being holy and near.
Tell him where you feel inadequate for what he asks, and ask him for his presence.
Ask him to help you go where he sends and speak what he gives.
